claims.source: Cells in the medial domain of the cephalic ganglion lobes expressed both pc2 and hh (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Some, but not all, hh+ cells express the cholinergic neuron marker chat.
claims.source: The cholinergic neuron marker Smed-choline acetyltransferase (chat) (Nishimura et al., 2010) was also expressed in some, but not all, hh+ cells (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Nishimura et al., 2010.

claims.claim: 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries.
claims.source: Differential expression analysis of cephalic ganglia versus head fragments following control RNAi revealed that, of the total 15,113 transcripts passing our filters (see methods), 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched and 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries (adjusted p-value <0.05, log2 fold change >1.0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries.
claims.source: Differential expression analysis of cephalic ganglia versus head fragments following control RNAi revealed that, of the total 15,113 transcripts passing our filters (see methods), 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched and 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries (adjusted p-value <0.05, log2 fold change >1.0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Broadly expressed neuronal markers syn, chat, and pc2 were only somewhat enriched in cephalic ganglia tissue.
claims.source: Broadly expressed neuronal markers syn, chat, and pc2 were only somewhat enriched (Figure 1E), consistent with the fact that these genes are also expressed in the peripheral nervous system located throughout the head.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and inference about peripheral nervous system expression.

claims.claim: Genes expressed in cells restricted to the medial CNS, such as hh and 1020HH, were more highly enriched at 57-fold and 81-fold, respectively.
claims.source: Conversely, genes expressed in cells restricted to the medial CNS, such as hh and the prohormone-encoding gene 1020HH (Collins et al., 2010) were more highly enriched, at 57-fold and 81-fold, respectively (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Collins et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Expression of hh in hh(RNAi) animals was significantly reduced.
claims.source: Expression of hh in hh(RNAi) animals was, as expected, significantly reduced (padj <0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: ptc expression was decreased in ptc(RNAi) animals as well as in hh(RNAi) animals.
claims.source: ptc expression was decreased in ptc(RNAi) animals as well as in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Hh acts by negatively regulating Patched protein, which in turn is a negative regulator of transcriptional targets of Hh signaling including the ptc gene itself.
claims.source: Hh acts by negatively regulating Patched protein, which in turn is a negative regulator of transcriptional targets of Hh signaling including the ptc gene itself (Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008.

claims.claim: The Hh signaling pathway is required for establishing expression domains of the transcription factors Nk2.2, Nk6.1, and Pax6 in the developing vertebrate neural tube.
claims.source: The Hh signaling pathway is required for establishing expression domains of the transcription factors Nk2.2, Nk6.1, and Pax6 in the developing vertebrate neural tube (Briscoe and Thérond, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Briscoe and Thérond, 2013.

claims.claim: Absence of SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate results in loss of cell types that normally form in these domains.
claims.source: Absence of SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate results in loss of cell types that normally form in these domains (Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2003.

claims.claim: In intact planarians, Hh signaling does not modulate expression domains of orthologous transcription factors nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b.
claims.source: By contrast, we were unable to find evidence that in intact planarians, which exhibit extensive tissue turnover and new cell type specification, Hh signaling modulates expression domains of orthologous transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1F) and FISH data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: The expression levels of nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b were not significantly changed in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals versus controls.
claims.source: The expression levels of Smed-nkx2 (nkx2), Smed-nkx6 (nkx6), and Smed-pax6b (pax6b) (Scimone et al., 2014a) were not significantly changed in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals versus controls (Figure 1F), and we confirmed this finding by FISH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1F), FISH data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and citation to Scimone et al., 2014a.

claims.claim: if-1 encodes a member of the cytoplasmic intermediate filament family.
claims.source: if-1 encodes a member of the cytoplasmic intermediate filament family (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Intermediate filaments are cytoskeletal proteins that provide structural support and mechanical stress resistance in a variety of cell types.
claims.source: Intermediate filaments are cytoskeletal proteins that provide structural support and mechanical stress resistance in a variety of cell types (Herrmann et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2007.

claims.claim: cali encodes a predicted protein with some similarity to vertebrate protocadherin PCDH19 but lacks clear cadherin domains.
claims.source: cali encodes a predicted protein with some similarity to vertebrate protocadherin PCDH19 but lacks clear cadherin domains (Frank and Kemler, 2002), and we therefore named this gene based on the morphology of the cells expressing it (see below).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to Frank and Kemler, 2002.

claims.claim: if-1 and cali are co-expressed primarily in cells in the neuropil of both the cephalic ganglia and the ventral nerve cords.
claims.source: FISH analysis revealed that if-1 and cali were co-expressed primarily in cells in the neuropil, the neurite-dense region surrounded by neuron cell bodies (Best and Noel, 1969; Morita and Best, 1965), of both the cephalic ganglia and the ventral nerve cords (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to Best and Noel, 1969; Morita and Best, 1965.

claims.claim: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil express ptc.
claims.source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil express ptc.
claims.source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: if-1+/cali+ cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling.
claims.source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ptc expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: if-1+/cali+ neuropil cells are adjacent to the hh+ neurons in the medial cortex.
claims.source: Additionally, if-1+/cali+ neuropil cells were adjacent to the hh+ neurons in the medial cortex, placing them in close proximity to a source of Hh ligand (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: if-1 and cali transcripts are detected in processes extending from the bodies of cells within the neuropil.
claims.source: if-1 and cali transcripts were detected in processes extending from the bodies of cells within the neuropil of both the cephalic ganglia and ventral nerve cords, indicating an elaborate morphology for these cells (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: Upon inhibition of hh, the density of if-1+/cali+ cells decreased both inside and outside the neuropil.
claims.source: Upon hh RNAi, the density of if-1+/cali+ cells decreased both inside and outside the neuropil (Figure 2H–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 2H-I.

claims.claim: The density of cells expressing either or both if-1 and cali in ptc(RNAi) animals increased slightly inside and considerably outside the neuropil.
claims.source: Accordingly, the density of cells expressing either or both if-1 and cali in ptc(RNAi) animals increased slightly inside and considerably outside the neuropil (Figure 2H–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 2H-I.

claims.claim: During regeneration, if-1+/cali+ cells accumulate in the blastema.
claims.source: During regeneration, if-1+/cali+ cells accumulated in the blastema, the outgrowth that forms at wounds and replaces missing tissue.
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: No if-1+/cali+ cells are observed in the blastema in hh(RNAi) animals.
claims.source: As expected, no if-1+/cali+ cells were observed in the blastema in hh(RNAi) animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: ptc(RNAi) anterior blastemas have a large number of if-1+/cali+ cells despite impaired head formation.
claims.source: Nonetheless, ptc(RNAi) anterior blastemas had a large number of if-1+/cali+ cells despite the impaired head formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of gli-1 results in loss of if-1 and cali signal.
claims.source: RNAi of gli-1 resulted in loss of if-1 and cali signal whereas RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 did not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 does not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali.
claims.source: RNAi of gli-1 resulted in loss of if-1 and cali signal whereas RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 did not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Hh signaling is required for if-1 and cali expression to be detected in the neuropil.
claims.source: We conclude that Hh signaling is required for if-1 and cali expression to be detected in the neuropil.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNAi experiments showing loss of if-1/cali expression upon hh and gli-1 inhibition.

claims.claim: pc2, chat, and syn are not expressed in any if-1+/cali+ cells.
claims.source: pc2, chat, and syn, three markers expressed broadly in planarian neurons, were not expressed in any if-1+/cali+ cells, raising the possibility that these cells are not neurons (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels, neurotransmitter synthesis enzymes, synaptic vesicle proteins, and neuronal transcription factors are not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
claims.source: Genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels, a potassium channel, a sodium channel, a calcium channel, a sodium and potassium co-transporter, Glutamic acid decarboxylase (gd), Tyrosine hydroxylase (th), Tryptophan hydroxylase (tph), three Synaptotagmin family members, Synaptogyrin 2, synaptic vesicle fusion proteins SNAP25 and Unc-13, the vesicular neurotransmitter transporters VAchT and VGluT, and neuronal transcription factors were all not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3D–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3D-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: netrin-2 is not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
claims.source: netrin-2, a marker previously described to be expressed in cells in the neuropil (Cebrià and Newmark, 2005), also was not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citation to Cebrià and Newmark, 2005.

claims.claim: if-1+/cali+ cells are not neurons.
claims.source: We conclude that, despite localization within the CNS and the presence of cytoplasmic extensions, if-1+/cali+ cells are not neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of neuronal marker expression in if-1+/cali+ cells.

claims.claim: gs is expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells in the ventral parenchyma and the intestine.
claims.source: Smed-gs (gs) encodes an ortholog of Glutamine Synthetase and was expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells in the ventral parenchyma and the intestine (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3I and WISH data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: eaat2-1 and eaat2-2 are expressed in the majority of if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil and to a lesser degree outside the neuropil.
claims.source: Two genes encoding orthologs of the glutamate transporter GLT-1/EAAT2 (Featherstone, 2011), Smed-eaat2-1 (eaat2-1) and Smed-eaat2-2 (eaat2-2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), were also expressed in the majority of if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil and to a lesser degree outside the neuropil (Figure 3J–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3J-K, phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and citation to Featherstone, 2011.

claims.claim: gat is expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
claims.source: Smed-gat (gat) is predicted to encode an ortholog of a family of GABA, creatine, and taurine transporters that are commonly used as invertebrate and vertebrate glia markers (Carducci et al., 2012; Featherstone, 2011; Minelli et al., 1996; Pow et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). gat was also expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3L, phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and citations to Carducci et al., 2012; Featherstone, 2011; Minelli et al., 1996; Pow et al., 2002.

claims.claim: glut is co-expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells outside the neuropil.
claims.source: We found a glucose transporter ortholog, Smed-glut (glut) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), co-expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells outside the neuropil (Figure 3M, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3M and phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: trpm is co-expressed with if-1 and cali in the neuropil, and expression is also observed in cells of the ventral parenchyma and pharynx.
claims.source: The expression pattern of trpm was similar to that of gs and gat; trpm was co-expressed with if-1 and cali in the neuropil, and expression was also observed in cells of the ventral parenchyma and pharynx (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3N and phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: gs+ cells outside the cephalic ganglia express gat, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, glut, and trpm.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that gs+ cells outside the cephalic ganglia expressed gat (Figure 3O), eaat2-1 (Figure 3P), eaat2-2 (Figure 3Q), glut (Figure 3R), and trpm (Figure 3S).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3O-S.

claims.claim: gs+ cells and glut+ cells outside the neuropil express ptc.
claims.source: We found that gs+ cells and glut+ cells outside the neuropil also expressed ptc, suggesting that at least a subset of the cells are competent to respond to Hh signaling (Figure 3T,U).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3T-U.

claims.claim: gs+ and eaat2-1+ cells outside the neuropil do not express pc2.
claims.source: To ensure that these cells outside the neuropil were not neurons, we performed double FISH for pc2 with gs or eaat2-1 and found no evidence of co-expression (Figure 3V,W).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3V-W.

claims.claim: Co-expression of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, and gat indicates that these cells function to reuptake and metabolize neurotransmitters.
claims.source: Co-expression of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, and gat indicates that these cells function to reuptake and metabolize neurotransmitters, a role performed in the vertebrate nervous system by astrocytes (Anderson and Swanson, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on marker co-expression and citation to Anderson and Swanson, 2000.

claims.claim: The cells expressing glial markers are hypothesized to be glia.
claims.source: Because these cells are embedded in the planarian nervous system and express glial markers rather than neuronal markers, we hypothesize that they are glia.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on molecular marker expression, localization, and morphology data.

claims.claim: RNAi of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, gat, glut, and trpm did not result in observable morphological or behavioral effects.
claims.source: To determine the role of these glia markers in planarian biology, we performed RNAi on gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, gat, glut, and trpm. However, we did not observe any morphological or behavioral effects in these animals during normal tissue turnover in uninjured animals and following head and tail amputation.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations following RNAi.

claims.claim: IF-1+ cellular extensions form an extensive network concentrated in the neuropil and extending out of the CNS.
claims.source: Whole-mount immunofluorescence revealed an extensive network of IF-1+ branches concentrated in the neuropil and extending out of the CNS (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: IF-1+ cellular extensions form hollow columns oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis.
claims.source: The IF-1+ cellular extensions also formed hollow columns oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: RNAi of if-1 results in complete loss of IF-1 antibody immunolabeling.
claims.source: RNAi of if-1 resulted in complete loss of IF-1 antibody immunolabeling, confirming that labeling was specific (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: IF-1+ processes emerging from the cephalic ganglion neuropil follow the same tracts as α-Tubulin+ axon bundles.
claims.source: The IF-1+ processes emerging from the cephalic ganglion neuropil followed the same tracts as the α-Tubulin+ axon bundles (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: IF-1+ processes are embedded within nerve bundles and do not appear to fully enclose the commissural axon fascicle.
claims.source: The IF-1+ processes were embedded within the nerve bundles and did not appear to fully enclose the commissural axon fascicle.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: IF-1+ processes weave through the synapse-dense cephalic ganglion neuropil.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence with both the anti-IF-1 antibody and the anti-Synapsin antibody showed IF-1+ processes weaving through the synapse-dense cephalic ganglion neuropil (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: IF-1+ processes appear to encapsulate and invade Synapsin+ clusters throughout the VNCs and the Orthogon.
claims.source: Moreover, IF-1+ processes appeared to encapsulate and invade Synapsin+ clusters throughout the VNCs and the Orthogon (Figure 4I–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claims.claim: Individual IF-1+ processes extend from one Synapsin+ cluster to another, indicating that single planarian glia can enwrap multiple targets.
claims.source: Individual IF-1+ processes also extended from one Synapsin+ cluster to another, indicating that single planarian glia can enwrap multiple targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: Inhibition of hh results in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal.
claims.source: Inhibition of hh resulted in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal and no change in expression or localization of Synapsin protein, whereas inhibition of ptc caused an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ptc causes an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal.
claims.source: Inhibition of hh resulted in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal and no change in expression or localization of Synapsin protein, whereas inhibition of ptc caused an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes.
claims.source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claims.claim: The percentage of orthogonal axon bundles associated with IF-1+ processes decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition.
claims.source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claims.claim: The percentage of orthogonal axon bundles associated with IF-1+ processes increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition.
claims.source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claims.claim: IF-1 protein perdures after if-1 mRNA is lost in hh(RNAi) animals.
claims.source: In hh(RNAi) animals we observed IF-1 protein by immunofluorescence despite the loss of detectable if-1 FISH signal throughout the neuropil, suggesting that hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia over the 12-day period during which we performed RNAi (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by combined FISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia.
claims.source: In hh(RNAi) animals we observed IF-1 protein by immunofluorescence despite the loss of detectable if-1 FISH signal throughout the neuropil, suggesting that hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia over the 12-day period during which we performed RNAi (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of IF-1 protein despite loss of if-1 mRNA.

claims.claim: Expression of gs, gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 is still observed throughout the neuropil in hh(RNAi) animals and is indistinguishable from control animals.
claims.source: Unlike the case for if-1 and cali, expression of the other glia markers was still observed throughout the neuropil and was indistinguishable from control animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ptc has no effect on the expression or localization of gs, gat, eaat2-1, or eaat2-2.
claims.source: Similarly, inhibition of ptc had no effect on the expression or localization of gs, gat, eaat2-1, or eaat2-2 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There is no significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals.
claims.source: We also did not observe a significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals, although the proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals.
claims.source: We also did not observe a significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals, although the proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: A large number of gat+/if-1+/cali+ cells are detected outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals despite no significant overall increase in the number of gat+ cells.
claims.source: Conversely, whereas a small proportion of gat+ glia outside the neuropil expressed if-1 and cali in control(RNAi) animals, a large number of gat+/if-1+/cali+ cells were detected outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals despite no significant overall increase in the number of gat+ cells (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: if-1 and cali are induced in planarian glia outside the neuropil when Hh signaling is activated by ptc inhibition.
claims.source: Given that planarian glia outside the neuropil also expressed ptc, these data suggest that if-1 and cali were induced in these cells when Hh signaling was activated by ptc inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increase in if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals.

claims.claim: Anterior blastemas of control(RNAi) animals after six days of regeneration contain cells expressing planarian glia markers.
claims.source: Anterior blastemas of control(RNAi) animals after six days of regeneration contained cells expressing planarian glia markers, both inside the forming neuropil and outside.
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In hh(RNAi) animals, expression of if-1 and cali is eliminated in blastemas, but cells expressing gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 are observed throughout the blastema.
claims.source: In hh(RNAi) animals, expression of if-1 and cali was eliminated, but cells expressing gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 were observed throughout the blastema (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The presence of glia markers in newly formed cells of the blastema suggests that the animal is capable of regenerating glia in the absence of Hh signaling.
claims.source: The presence of these markers in newly formed cells of the blastema suggests that the animal is capable of regenerating glia in the absence of Hh signaling.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of glia marker expression in hh(RNAi) blastemas.

claims.claim: An increase in the number of if-1+/cali+ cells is observed in ptc(RNAi) animals despite irradiation.
claims.source: By contrast, we observed an increase in the number of if-1+/cali+ cells in ptc(RNAi) animals despite irradiation (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 6A-C.

claims.claim: The ectopic if-1+/cali+ cells outside of the neuropil in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals have branches.
claims.source: The ectopic if-1+/cali+ cells outside of the neuropil in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals had branches, indicating that ectopic expression occurred in existing cells with complex morphology (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil is similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, the total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil was similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals, but the proportion of glut+ cells that expressed if-1 and cali was higher following RNAi of ptc (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The proportion of glut+ cells that express if-1 and cali is higher in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, the total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil was similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals, but the proportion of glut+ cells that expressed if-1 and cali was higher following RNAi of ptc (Figure 6D).

results.result: RNA sequencing of dissected cephalic ganglia tissue successfully enriched for CNS-associated transcripts. The dissection protocol yielded 2237 significantly enriched and 1938 significantly diminished transcripts in cephalic ganglia versus head fragments, with CNS-restricted genes like hh and 1020HH showing 57-fold and 81-fold enrichment respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C38-C41 collectively demonstrate successful tissue-specific RNA-seq methodology. The differential expression analysis (C38-C39) and validation with known CNS markers (C40-C41) provide converging evidence that the dissection protocol effectively enriched for CNS transcripts, establishing the foundation for subsequent gene discovery.

results.result: hh is expressed in medial cephalic ganglia neurons that co-express the neuronal marker pc2 and partially overlap with cholinergic neurons expressing chat. This expression pattern is spatially analogous to the vertebrate neural tube floor plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25, C36-C37 are supported by double FISH data (Figure 1A-B) and prior literature. The co-expression analysis with neuronal markers definitively establishes the neuronal identity of hh+ cells and their medial localization, though the analogy to vertebrate floor plate (C26) is inferential.

results.result: Two genes, if-1 (encoding a cytoplasmic intermediate filament) and cali (encoding a protocadherin-like protein), were identified as misregulated by Hh signaling and are co-expressed in non-neural cells within the CNS neuropil.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C49, C51-C52 are well-supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1G), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and FISH localization (Figure 2A-B). The identification of these genes as Hh-responsive and their characterization as non-neural based on localization is robust.

results.result: Hh signaling perturbation does not affect expression of orthologous transcription factors nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b in intact planarians, contrasting with the role of Hh in establishing transcription factor domains in vertebrate neural tube development.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43, C47-C48 are supported by RNA-seq (Figure 1F) and FISH validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The lack of significant changes in transcription factor expression following hh and ptc RNAi is clearly demonstrated, establishing a key difference from vertebrate CNS patterning.

results.result: if-1+/cali+ cells express the Hh receptor ptc and are spatially adjacent to hh+ neurons, indicating they are competent to respond to Hh signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by double FISH data (Figure 2C-D) showing high percentages of ptc co-expression (97.8% inside neuropil, 100% outside) and spatial proximity to hh+ neurons. This establishes the cellular basis for Hh-mediated regulation of these cells.

results.result: Hh signaling through gli-1 is required for if-1 and cali expression in the neuropil. hh RNAi decreases if-1+/cali+ cell density, while ptc RNAi increases it, and gli-1 (but not gli-2 or gli-3) RNAi phenocopies hh loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59, C63-C65 are supported by FISH quantification (Figure 2H-I) and gli RNAi experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The opposing effects of hh and ptc inhibition, consistent with canonical Hh signaling, and the specific requirement for gli-1 provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: if-1+/cali+ cells do not express neuronal markers including pc2, chat, syn, voltage-gated ion channels, neurotransmitter synthesis enzymes, synaptic vesicle proteins, or neuronal transcription factors, establishing that these cells are not neurons despite their CNS localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are comprehensively supported by extensive double FISH analysis (Figure 3A-H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The systematic exclusion of multiple classes of neuronal markers provides strong evidence that if-1+/cali+ cells represent a distinct non-neuronal cell type.

results.result: if-1+/cali+ cells express orthologs of astrocyte-associated genes involved in neurotransmitter uptake and metabolism, including gs (glutamine synthetase), eaat2-1 and eaat2-2 (glutamate transporters), gat (GABA transporter), glut (glucose transporter), and trpm (ion channel).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74, C78 are supported by double FISH data (Figure 3I-N) and phylogenetic analyses confirming orthology (Figure 3—figure supplements 3-6). The co-expression of multiple functionally related genes involved in neurotransmitter metabolism provides strong molecular evidence for a glial identity.

results.result: Cells expressing glial markers (gs, gat, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, glut, trpm) exist outside the cephalic ganglia neuropil, express ptc, and do not express neuronal markers, indicating a broadly distributed population of glia-like cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by double FISH data (Figure 3O-W) showing co-expression of glial markers outside the neuropil, ptc expression in these cells, and absence of pc2 co-expression. This extends the glial population beyond the CNS proper.

results.result: The if-1+/cali+ cells are proposed to be planarian glia based on their molecular marker expression, CNS localization, non-neuronal identity, and expression of genes involved in neurotransmitter metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C79 represent the central hypothesis supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: non-neuronal identity (C66-C69), expression of astrocyte-associated genes (C70-C74), CNS localization (C52), and morphology (C57, C81-C87). While functional validation is limited (C80), the molecular and morphological evidence strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: IF-1 protein localizes to an extensive network of cellular processes concentrated in the neuropil, following axon tracts, and closely associating with synaptic regions. These processes weave through synapse-dense areas and appear to encapsulate synaptic glomeruli.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82, C84-C88 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 4A-K, Figure 4—figure supplements) including expansion microscopy (Videos 1-8). The detailed morphological characterization demonstrates the intimate association of IF-1+ processes with neuronal structures, supporting a glial support function.

results.result: Hh signaling regulates IF-1 protein levels and distribution. hh inhibition eliminates IF-1 signal, while ptc inhibition increases IF-1+ process association with orthogonal axon bundles from 15.1% to 61.4%.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification (Figure 4L, N). The opposing effects of hh and ptc inhibition on IF-1 protein distribution, with quantitative assessment of axon bundle association, provide strong evidence for Hh-dependent regulation of glial morphology.

results.result: IF-1 protein perdures after if-1 mRNA is lost in hh(RNAi) animals, suggesting that hh RNAi impacts transcription in existing glia rather than causing cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by combined FISH and immunofluorescence data (Figure 5A) showing persistence of IF-1 protein despite loss of if-1 mRNA. This temporal dissociation between mRNA and protein loss provides evidence that Hh regulates gene expression rather than cell survival.

results.result: Hh signaling specifically regulates if-1 and cali expression without affecting other glial markers (gs, gat, eaat2-1, eaat2-2) or total glia cell numbers. ptc inhibition induces if-1 and cali in existing glia outside the neuropil.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 are supported by double FISH data and quantification (Figure 5B-C). The selective effect on if-1/cali versus other glial markers, maintenance of total gat+ cell numbers, and increased if-1+/cali+ proportion in ptc(RNAi) demonstrate that Hh regulates glial gene expression state rather than cell fate or number.

results.result: Irradiation experiments demonstrate that ptc inhibition induces if-1 and cali expression in existing mature glia. Despite blocking new cell production, ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals show increased if-1+/cali+ cells with branched morphology, and increased proportion of glut+ cells expressing if-1/cali without change in total glut+ cell number.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 are supported by FISH data and quantification in irradiated animals (Figure 6A-D). The persistence of ectopic if-1/cali expression despite irradiation, presence of branches in ectopic cells, and unchanged total glut+ cell numbers provide strong evidence that Hh signaling dynamically regulates gene expression in mature glia based on proximity to hh+ neurons.

results.result: Planarian glia are distributed broadly throughout the animal but only express if-1 and cali in the neuropil near hh+ neurons, indicating spatial regulation of glial gene expression by Hh signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by FISH data showing broad distribution of gs+, gat+, and other marker+ cells (Figure 3O-S) but restricted if-1/cali expression near hh+ neurons (Figure 2D, H-I). This spatial pattern, combined with the irradiation experiments (C105-C111), establishes that Hh signaling creates distinct glial states based on proximity to the Hh source.

results.result: This study provides the first molecular and morphological evidence for glia in planarians and demonstrates that Hh signaling regulation of CNS glia is a common feature across all three superphyla of the Bilateria.
results.evaluation: Claims C113 and C137 represent the major conclusions supported by the comprehensive molecular, morphological, and functional characterization of planarian glia (C7-C88) and comparison with Hh signaling roles in vertebrate and Drosophila glia (C32-C35, C114-C119, C129-C131). The novelty claim is supported by prior literature showing only morphological descriptions without molecular evidence (C112).

results.result: RNAi of glial marker genes (gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, gat, glut, trpm) did not result in observable morphological or behavioral phenotypes during homeostasis or regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by experimental observations, though the lack of phenotype is a negative result. This suggests either functional redundancy, incomplete knockdown, or that the assays used were not sensitive enough to detect subtle defects. The claim is accurately stated as an observation rather than a definitive conclusion about gene function.

results.result: During regeneration, glia markers are present in blastemas. In hh(RNAi) animals, if-1 and cali expression is eliminated but other glial markers (gat, eaat2-1, eaat2-2) are still expressed, suggesting glia can regenerate in the absence of Hh signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by FISH data in regenerating blastemas (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The differential effect on if-1/cali versus other glial markers in hh(RNAi) blastemas is consistent with the homeostatic findings and suggests that while Hh regulates specific glial genes, it is not required for glial cell regeneration per se.

results.result: During regeneration, if-1+/cali+ cells accumulate in control blastemas but are absent in hh(RNAi) blastemas. ptc(RNAi) anterior blastemas contain many if-1+/cali+ cells despite impaired head formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by FISH data in regenerating animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). These observations extend the Hh-dependent regulation of if-1/cali to the regeneration context and show that ectopic Hh signaling can induce these markers even in malformed tissue.

results.result: The regulation of intermediate filament proteins by Hh signaling in glia and the ability for neurons to instruct glial gene expression profiles are striking commonalities between planarians and vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C117 and C119 are supported by comparison of the planarian findings with vertebrate literature (C115-C116, C118). While the specific genes and functional contexts differ, the parallel regulatory mechanisms represent meaningful evolutionary conservation. The comparative analysis is appropriately qualified as identifying commonalities rather than claiming identical mechanisms.

results.result: Regionalized expression of orthologs of Hh-responsive vertebrate neural tube transcription factors appears unaffected by Hh signaling in uninjured planarians, consistent with the possibility that Hh signaling was co-opted into a dorsal-ventral patterning role in the deuterostome lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by RNA-seq and FISH data (C47-C48) and comparative analysis with Drosophila and Platynereis (C122-C124). The evolutionary inference (C126) is appropriately presented as speculative, and the data support the conclusion that Hh does not pattern the planarian CNS in the same way it patterns the vertebrate neural tube.

results.result: A shared function of Hh signaling among Deuterostomes, Ecdysozoans, and Lophotrochozoans is in the control of glia near the midline.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 is supported by the planarian findings combined with comparative analysis of Hh roles in vertebrate floor plate glia (C127-C128) and Drosophila midline glia (C129-C130). This represents a synthesis of the current work with existing literature to identify a conserved ancestral function of Hh signaling in bilaterian CNS development.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about Hh signaling roles in vertebrate and invertebrate CNS development, planarian biology, and glial functions in other organisms.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C14-C24, C27-C35, C44-C46, C50, C114-C116, C118, C120-C124, C127-C130, C132-C134) represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. They provide essential context for interpreting the novel findings but are not themselves results of this study.

results.result: The expression of hh in medial cephalic ganglia neurons suggests a possible role in CNS maintenance or regeneration, and this location is analogous to the vertebrate neural tube floor plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C26 are speculative inferences based on expression patterns. While the spatial analogy to the floor plate is reasonable based on medial positioning, the functional implications remain uncertain. The study does not directly test CNS maintenance or regeneration functions of hh in neurons, focusing instead on its role in regulating glial gene expression.

results.result: patched (ptc) encodes the Hh receptor.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 is established knowledge about the Hedgehog signaling pathway, well-supported by the literature. This is a factual statement about pathway components.

results.result: RNAi of if-1 results in complete loss of IF-1 antibody immunolabeling, confirming antibody specificity.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). This is an important control demonstrating that the IF-1 antibody specifically recognizes the IF-1 protein, validating all subsequent immunofluorescence experiments.

results.result: Previous electron microscopy studies identified candidate planarian glia based on localization and appearance but did not provide molecular evidence.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by citations to Golubev, 1988 and Morita and Best, 1966. This accurately characterizes prior work and establishes the novelty of the current molecular characterization.

results.result: IF-1+ processes are not seen deviating from axonal tracts and perturbations affecting gene regulation in planarian glia do not result in observable disruption to the neural network.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 are supported by immunofluorescence observations and RNAi phenotype analysis. These observations support the hypothesis that planarian glia passively extend into existing neural architecture rather than actively patterning it, though this remains somewhat speculative without more direct functional tests.
